tasks.name: stability
tasks.title: Silence in, silence out
tasks.description: With no sensory drive the network must not spontaneously light up. A model whose gain is too high "passes" every reflex because everything fires; this task is the guard against that. (Real flies do have spontaneous activity — the LIF model has none by construction, so quiet is the correct answer here.)
tasks.citation: Shiu et al. 2024, Nature — model is silent without input by design

tasks.name: sugar_to_proboscis
tasks.title: Sugar → proboscis extension
tasks.description: The canonical reflex. Activating sugar-sensing gustatory receptor neurons should drive MN9, the motor neuron that extends the proboscis. This is the headline result of Shiu et al. 2024 and a behaviour every fly lab can reproduce with a drop of sucrose.

tasks.name: bitter_suppression
tasks.title: Bitter suppresses the sugar response
tasks.description: Co-activating bitter GRNs with sugar GRNs should reduce MN9 output relative to sugar alone. Flies reject sucrose laced with quinine; the connectome should show why (bitter-driven inhibition onto the sugar pathway).
tasks.citation: Shiu et al. 2024 (Nature) Fig. 3; Jaeger et al. 2018

tasks.name: looming_to_giant_fiber
tasks.title: Looming → giant fiber escape
tasks.description: LPLC2 and LC4 are the visual projection neurons that detect an expanding (looming) object. They converge on the Giant Fiber, the descending neuron that triggers the takeoff escape. Drive the detectors; the GF should fire.
tasks.citation: von Reyn et al. 2014; Ache et al. 2019; Shiu et al. 2024

tasks.name: taste_specificity
tasks.title: Bitter alone does not extend the proboscis
tasks.description: A negative control. Bitter GRNs alone should not drive MN9; if they do, the model has lost the sign of its inhibitory synapses or the gain is high enough that any input reaches any output.

tasks.name: dose_response
tasks.title: Proboscis response scales with sugar intensity
tasks.description: Real flies extend the proboscis more reliably and more strongly as sucrose concentration rises; GRN firing rate encodes concentration. A model whose MN9 output is all-or-nothing (saturating at the refractory limit the moment any input arrives) has lost that gradation. Weak drive (20 Hz on the sugar GRNs) should give a clearly smaller MN9 response than strong drive (100 Hz), and both should be above baseline.
tasks.citation: Dethier 1976; Dahanukar et al. 2007 (Neuron); Shiu et al. 2024

tasks.name: adaptation
tasks.title: Repeated sugar gives a smaller second response
tasks.description: Sensory responses adapt: a second identical sugar pulse shortly after the first evokes a weaker proboscis response (short-term adaptation in GRNs and downstream circuits; over longer timescales, PER habituation). A memoryless point-neuron model cannot do this by construction — every pulse looks like the first — so the reference LIF is expected to fail here. That is the point: this task measures something the wiring diagram alone does not give you.
tasks.citation: Duerr & Quinn 1982 (PNAS, PER habituation); Paranjpe et al. 2012 (J. Neurosci.)

tasks.name: olfactory_sparse_coding
tasks.title: One odour channel stays one channel
tasks.description: Olfactory receptor neurons of a single glomerulus (DA1, the cVA pheromone channel) synapse onto their own projection neurons. Lateral inhibition by local neurons keeps the antennal lobe output sparse: driving DA1 ORNs should fire DA1 PNs strongly while most PNs of the other ~50 glomeruli stay quiet, and the third-order lateral horn should not light up wholesale. A model with the wrong excitation/inhibition balance turns one odour into "all odours".
tasks.citation: Olsen & Wilson 2008 (Nature); Wilson 2013 (Annu. Rev. Neurosci.); Kohl et al. 2013

tasks.name: crosstalk
tasks.title: Taste does not trigger escape; looming does not trigger feeding
tasks.description: Negative controls across circuits. Sugar on the labellum should not fire the Giant Fiber, and a looming shadow should not extend the proboscis. Both circuits pass their own reflex tests in the core tier; this task asks whether they stay separate, which fails when the global gain is high enough that activity spreads through shared interneurons.
tasks.citation: von Reyn et al. 2014; Shiu et al. 2024

tasks.name: looming_dn_ensemble
tasks.title: Looming recruits the takeoff ensemble, not the whole descending tract
tasks.description: The Giant Fiber is not alone: looming also drives DNp02, DNp11 and other descending neurons that prepare the takeoff (leg extension, wing raise), and the response is selective — a few dozen of the ~1300 descending neurons, not a general alarm. Checks that the named looming DNs fire and that the descending population as a whole stays mostly silent.
tasks.citation: Ache et al. 2019 (Curr. Biol.); Namiki et al. 2018 (eLife); Dombrovski et al. 2023 (Nature)

tasks.name: flash_is_not_loom
tasks.title: A uniform flash is not a looming object
tasks.description: LPLC2/LC4 respond to expanding edges, not to the whole eye lighting up. Driving every photoreceptor at once (a full-field flash) should therefore not fire the Giant Fiber the way looming does. In a pure connectome model motion selectivity has to emerge from the lamina/medulla circuitry and the synaptic delays alone — no dendritic nonlinearities, no adaptation — so this is expected to be hard. Failure here means the model's visual front end is a brightness detector, which is worth knowing before wiring it to a game.
tasks.citation: von Reyn et al. 2014 (Nat. Neurosci.); Card & Dickinson 2008 (Curr. Biol.); Klapoetke et al. 2017 (Nature)

tasks.name: return_to_rest
tasks.title: The brain goes quiet again after the stimulus ends
tasks.description: A real fly tastes sugar, extends its proboscis, and a second later is at rest again. In this model a half-second taste of sugar leaves ~8% of the brain firing at a constant rate indefinitely: recurrent excitation sustains itself and nothing in a static wiring diagram with five constants can switch it off (no spike-frequency adaptation, no short-term synaptic depression, no neuromodulation). This task stimulates for 500 ms, then measures 1–1.3 s after the stimulus stopped. It is the clearest single number for "what a wiring diagram is missing".
tasks.citation: Dethier 1976 (PER duration); Shiu et al. 2024 (activity tracks stimulus); Benda & Herz 2003 (adaptation)
